A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IMPspec by the same authors, despite the changed title and extensive reorganization. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and proofs, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results for causal uncertainty quantification, ablations, and causal Bayesian optimization, including a healthcare simulator, generally over 50 trials.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports an additional Continuous DR comparison on the synthetic benchmark.

M1.justification: The reformulated priors retain the core IMPspec construction, posterior moments, and Gaussian approximation. However, v2 corrects the displayed training losses: the outcome likelihood uses sigma squared, and the weighted likelihood includes noise in the log determinant and corrects the trace term (v1 Equations 36–38; v2 Equations 20–21). These are limited formula corrections; implementation changes are not established.

E1.justification: The toy data-fusion task, synthetic CATE and ATT tasks, out-of-distribution evaluation, and healthcare optimization simulation are retained. Renaming the toy variables from Z/X to A/M does not change coverage. The removed approximation ablation used the existing toy scenario.

E2.justification: v2 adds Kennedy et al. (2017), labeled Continuous DR, to the synthetic benchmark in Table 2 and Figure 4. Mercer and random-Fourier posterior approximations disappear with v1 Figure 8. The other benchmark and Bayesian optimization comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Synthetic Table 2 switches from the earlier overall RMSE reporting to explicitly in-distribution RMSE over treatment values in [-2.5, 2.5]. v2 separately specifies the out-of-distribution calibration ranges. The retained experiments keep their sample sizes, training budgets, sample-splitting settings, and ten-iteration optimization horizon.

E4.justification: v2 removes the posterior-approximation validation comparing Gaussian projection with Mercer and random-Fourier truncations (v1 Figure 8). Sample-splitting and BayesIMP kernel ablations remain in Table 4. v2 adds a prior-sampling comparison with a standard GP and revises the kernel-basis illustration.

E5.justification: The toy experiment's reported outer credible-band level changes from 95% in v1 Figure 2 to 90% in v2 Figure 3. Otherwise, 50-trial reporting, mean and standard deviation tables, and 100 bootstrap replications for calibration uncertainty are retained; no increased run count is stated.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds Continuous DR results: RMSE 0.605±0.321 and calibration errors 0.131±0.023 in distribution and 0.112±0.032 outside it. IMPspec's table RMSE changes from 0.517±0.192 to 0.361±0.158 under the revised aggregation, so this is not a same-setting gain. Tables 1, 3, and 4 retain their values, while v1's posterior-approximation comparison results are removed.

T1.justification: v1's general Hilbert-space regression extension and spectral-coefficient posterior theorem are replaced by an isonormal-GP framework, new expectation-interchange and representation proofs, and substantially rewritten posterior derivations. v2 revises topological and characteristic-kernel assumptions and adds formal kernel-tail propositions. The posterior-moment formulas and calibration-consistency result remain, with the latter moved to Theorem 6.

C1.justification: v1 presents extending Hilbert-space regression theory as a central contribution in its abstract and introduction. v2 withdraws that contribution and centers its account on function-class expansion, continuous-treatment modeling, and tractable inference and calibration algorithms. Claims of strong uncertainty-quantification and optimization performance remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation of the IMPspec prior as heavier-tailed than a standard GP and develops more specific kernel-decay explanations for underfitting and variance collapse. It removes v1's discussion of the approximation-validation evidence. The main interpretations of the retained benchmark and optimization results remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and explicit inference, calibration, and data-fusion pseudocode, while removing the Mercer/RFF posterior-sampling instructions from v1 Appendix A.4. Existing experimental hyperparameters largely remain. The new calibration pseudocode conflicts with the retained sample-splitting implementation description, and the added Continuous DR baseline lacks a corresponding implementation paragraph.

R1.justification: v2 adds continuous-treatment doubly robust positioning through Kennedy et al. (2017) and Semenova and Chernozhukov (2021), plus supporting GP and kernel-regression references. It drops Knapik et al. (2011) and other sources associated with the removed theoretical framework. Its principal relationships to Singh et al. (2024), BayesIMP, and Bayesian calibration remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and much of the technical exposition are rewritten. Background topics are reordered, inference and training receive separate sections, related work moves later, and experiments adopt clearer experiment/results divisions. The appendices are extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds the prior-sample figure and three algorithm displays, redraws causal diagrams and experimental plots, and changes legends, axes, captions, and table headings. Experimental DAGs and optimization curves move to the appendix, while the factorization diagram and approximation-ablation figure disappear. These are substantial visual and layout revisions.

improvement.justification: v2 improves exposition, supplies code-access information, corrects likelihood formulas, and adds a relevant frequentist comparator. However, it removes direct posterior-approximation validation and introduces reliability problems: Algorithm 2 checks each bootstrap mean against its own centered interval, making coverage trivial and contradicting Appendix C.1.3; Proposition 2's proof reverses the inequality implied by log-convexity. These correctness and reproducibility concerns offset clear communication gains, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
